SAFA - A Legacy Plundered

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In 2010, SA’s football loving nation was given the gift of hope – A Legacy Trust Fund– meant to develop the beautiful game. How did that 450 million rand become SAFA’s cash cow, milked dry?

Unique Selling Point:
The beans on SAFA’s mismanagement and bad governance have been spilled. With a virtually bankrupt balance sheet and a failure to develop football from ground up to National level, its President and chief for over a decade, Danny Jordaan, remains untouchable, winning election after election. How does he stay in control? Whistleblowers that have been victim to his manipulation speak out on camera. We don’t stop there, we expose how the rot has permeated the development of football at grass root level. Young football stars and wannabes who have been failed by the very body that is supposed to uplift them and the game.

Summary:
2010 was the year South Africa hosted the first FIFA World Cup held in Africa. A year of hope and optimism for a nation of soccer lovers. The reward from FIFA was 450 million rand in the form of a Legacy Trust Fund. Money that was meant to develop and support the game. Treasurer of the World Cup Committee at the time, Mohammed Mubarak, says it was a living annuity that should have earned interest in perpetuity. The interest generated year on year would have been enough to keep the development going, without touching the capital.

In October 2021, the Legacy Trust Fund ran dry, closing its books with Five Million rand in the bank. SAFA sent its trustees packing without even a look-see at the final balance sheet. This was similar to the closure of the World Cup Committee in 2010, who never got to see the final balance sheets after the games ended. Carte Blanche exposes how a self-interested president, Danny Jordaan, has abused his authority and manipulated his stay in power at the expense of SAFA, putting at risk its ultimate goal - to support, uplift and develop the game of football in South Africa.

How the Legacy Trust Fund was plundered and used as a cash cow for SAFA’s deteriorating balance sheet:
As sponsors pulled out, after alleged rape charges against Danny Jordaan, so the Legacy Trust was dipped into more and more. And what was meant to be the jewel in the crown, the development of a world class training centre at Fun Valley Resort, South of Johannesburg, unearthed the rot. A controversial 67 million rand purchase that’s not fit for purpose and may never be. Again the Legacy Trust was used to fund this venture. But down the line the fallout reaches across the country, as aspirant young players are left to play on dusty pitches, with no kits or prizes, no transport to get to games - caught in a system that is crushing their football dreams. A system that mirrors the mother body in every way, where administrators hold on to power for perks and holidays, silencing detractors along the way. An old adage says: “The fish smells from the head”.


Further information:
Bart Henderson has been a forensic auditor for over 30 years. He lectures at the University of Pretoria and has worked on many prominent fraud and government corruption cases over the years. He uses data analysis to create a profile of the person(s) he is investigating. His mantra is – “I treat every sentence as a crime scene”.

Bart has been involved in investigating the SAFA Legacy Trust Fund that was handed to SAFA after the 2010 World Cup - around R450 million Rand. He is baying for justice for the young up-and-coming sports stars that should have benefited from this legacy fund.

The whistle-blowers which involve previous SAFA CEOs, Legacy Trust trustees and members of the NEC, allege they have been ignored or shut down by President of SAFA Danny Jordaan, and the CFO Gronie Hluyo over the years.

The Legacy Trust was wound up in October 2021 without giving a final account of the remaining funds of 40 million Rands to the trustees, as they were relieved of their duties before it was wound up. Former SAFA Vice President and Legacy Trust trustee Ria Ledwaba says she has never seen the paperwork and when she requested it, she was told that she was no longer a trustee. According to her she never signed off the trust and if you look at the Master’s papers she is still listed as a trustee.

According to Henderson, SAFA will not disclose a paper trail of how the funds were used for the Legacy Trust. The purchase of the Fun Valley Resort as a Training facility has been steeped in controversy. It was bought for a reported 67 million rand, but valued at 30 to 40. The deal was done through Ernst and Young and Cohen who was the seller – they, to this day, have not been able to produce evidence of where the money was deposited. There is a Hawks investigation that is ongoing and arrests were expected to be made a few years back, but nothing has happened. Former CEO Dennis Mumble gives a first hand account on how this property was purchased and how, after warning Danny Jordaan that it was a dud deal, he was shut out and the deal was put through.

The Training Centre is not fit for purpose, and the South African official teams refuse to stay there. It apparently is only used occasionally for youth training programmes. It was supposed to be a world class training facility.

Former Treasurer of the World Cup Committee, Mohammed Mubarak, attests to the purpose of the Legacy Trust and how it could have been the real saviour of football in South Africa, instead it was milked dry. He reflects on his brushings with Jordaan at the time and how when he was the treasurer of the World Cup Committee, he too was shut out when it came time to see the final balance sheets and bank statements. Even though he had resigned he remained treasurer to the end.

SAFA has posted on their website, discrediting or trying to discredit Henderson. It is alleging that “former disgruntled officials of SAFA”, Henderson and a former trustee are trying to scupper the bid for the Women’s World Cup in 2027. It appears that this is the way that SAFA deals with detractors, they don’t answer questions from the media, even going as far as banning Daily Maverick and by attacking anyone who is exposing malfeasance.

Henderson is not alone, there are many members who have served at SAFA willing to speak of the governance and alleged fraudulent activities conducted by SAFA under Danny Jordaan.

For example according to Henderson, the current NEC has 47 members all of whom get paid a hundred thousand rand a year. They are merely there to be able to vote in SAFAs elections. In no other country are there so many NEC members, there are normally around 15, and FIFA recommended a reduction to 18, but that has never occurred. SAFA says they are cash strapped yet are not willing to make that kind of reduction, why? There has been an irregular turnover of CEOs, acting CEOs and Vice Presidents over the last few years, the question is why? The answer lies hidden in the loss of institutional memory. It’s harder for the naysayers to fight back.

Money that is supposed to have been distributed to the regions for development purposes through the trust appears to still be outstanding, and the way the figures are put out fudge what is from the Legacy Trust and what is coming from SAFA’s obligatory contributions, according to Ria Ledwaba, a former SAFA Vice President and trustee of the Legacy Trust Fund.

According to Mubarak and Henderson the Legacy Trust should have been a living trust where the original amount should not have been touched. If it had been put in a fixed deposit at 10% it would have earned 47 million a year that could go into development without touching the original funds. Yet now the Legacy Trust was depleted and closed with no public money trail.

On the ground, virtually every region we spoke to at grass roots level is crying for support and grants from SAFA. In most cases they are afraid to speak out for fear of retribution, but one passionate excommunicated coach, Thabo Rabalao, is not afraid. He’s willing to put himself on the line for his teams and his players. Situated in the North West, in Zeerust, he gives us an inside view of the challenges he and his players face. The lack of facilities, sponsorship, kits and prizes, something that there used to be before. That after an illegal suspension, his young players are left with no leagues to play in. And that no one from the region right through to National even cares to respond to him after multiple appeals. We speak to one of his talented young players who feels that all his dreams are dashed. They even missed a selection a few weeks back because they are suspended and don’t have valid SAFA cards. We ask the question, why is there no legacy and no support for the footballers of the future? What role should SAFA be playing?

SAFA is steeped in controversy and alleged misgovernance, with alleged fraudulent activity around Fun Valley and allegations by its former members. The collateral damage is to “football”. We put these serious questions to the man at the helm, its President, Danny Jordaan.

TREATMENT

Treatment Summary:

The story will be told through the central character – SAFA’s white elephant - Fun Valley. 38 Hectares of land, nestled between Lenasia and Soweto, a dream in the making, a hotel, refurbished rooms, a football pitch or two, this is the 87 million rand or so home - for the South African Football Association’s Technical Centre purchased in 2015. The vision – A world class Technical Training Facility able to host National and international teams.

As in knockout football tournaments, the visual device I want to use is the presenter putting their hand in a bag.. as in picking a draw.. and pulling out a ball.

Each ball has a name on it – and each ‘fixture’ will highlight key issues – eg ‘Danny Jordaan vs the Legacy Trust’. ‘Mumble vs Jordaan’, etc.. The presenter calls the draw, and each ‘match’ is an element of the story we are highlighting - turns to another camera to take us back into the narrative.. audio with audio transitions of football crowds cheering .. singing or jeering in disappointment..

The links will be done in a studio-like setting… as one would a draw..

Visual narrative will be built through three teenagers kicking a soccer ball down a dusty road – two boys and a girl – the scenes will be moody and dark.. often just focusing on their faces .. when we talk about legacy or development.. a slow-mo shot of a football tumbling through the air.. etc.. With some possible archive of football matches from SuperSport as well?

We also have paper trail evidence – minutes of meetings etc.. emails to back what the whistle-blowers are saying.

Some recreations/ dramatisations – nuanced and not overt – that reflect some of the dealings behind closed doors etc...


ACT 1

We take a stay for a night at Fun Valley, although it may be fit for a tourist for a night or two, it currently does not have nearly the facilities and amenities to make it world class.
But is it and when will it ever be fit for purpose?

Dennis Mumble VP under Danny Jordaan was the man instructed to conclude the deal. Dennis describes the circumstances that led to a purchase of a property that cost double the evaluation price. He takes a journey with us to Fun Valley, here he describes how Cohen the seller, after the poor valuation told him to take the deal or leave it.

Presenter Link – Draw – Mumble vs Jordaan

Mumble highlights to Jordaan why this is a bad deal and it is overpriced. How Jordaan bull-dosed the deal through the NEC and the Trust without due diligence or adhering to proper corporate governance. ( First hand account)

This story is backed by Shuping Seboko who served as a member of the NEC at the time.

Ria Ledwaba – Trustee and Former VP of SAFA – backs this up on how it was announced at a Trustee meeting that the NEC had approved the purchase of the property and that the trust was to make the money available – the normal practice is for SAFA to apply to the Trust for funding. This did not occur – nor was there a discussion with the NEC about the purchase – it was announced at the NEC that the funds had been made available by the Trust for this purpose – to buy Fun Valley.


ACT 2

Our story will take us back to 2010 where the Legacy Trust was formed and its intended purpose. Here Mohammed Mubarak the treasurer of the SAFA 2010 Committee – gives us the inside track and we see how history repeats itself –

VO: Since the 2010 World Cup that put South Africa centre stage – SAFA has been mired in controversy – at its helm Chairman Danny Jordaan.

Presenter Link: putting his hand in a black bag and mixing the balls – presenter makes the draw and reads:

“[Mokoena?/] Mubarak” .. “vesus” .. “Jordaan”

[Mokoena?/] Mubarak - treasurer of the 2010 World Cup Committee, talks about how devastating the bribery allegations have been to SAFA and how he was shut out before the final financial tally after the World Cup ended, even though he had been the treasurer throughout. He talks about how, then, Danny Jordaan started shaping his fiefdom, removing all detractors and scrutinisors. He throws forward to the Legacy Trust that should have kept football alive if only they had just used the 10% interest generated annually from the 450 million – it could still be in existence.

He was relieved of his duties as treasurer of the 2010 World Cup Committee before the final financial tallies were made.. even though he had resigned, Mubarak remained treasurer until the end, but was never allowed to see the books he had administered.

Here Mubarak talks passionately about the development of football in South Africa, and how SAFA has misused the Legacy Trust..

MOKOENA: Former VP and acting CEO: SAFA

RIA: talks about the irregular way the trust was closed and how she never got to see the final financials, as the trustees were relieved of their positions before that was done. The only Trustee left to wind things up was not even someone with a financial background. FIFA was unhappy with how it was done and there are emails to prove this.

The trust was dissolved in 2021 with only five million Rand in the kitty –

Presenter link – the draw: SAFA vs Development

Thabo Rabalao is a club owner of an LFA in Zeerust, North West Province. He is passionate about the development of youth football. Due to a disagreement with the Region, he and his teams have been suspended from the SAFA leagues for over 7 months. This is unconstitutional according to the LFA and regional constitution which states that a team or person cannot be suspended for longer than 3 months if a matter has not been resolved. Thabo describes how the regional SAFA officials are not interested in developing the game, especially in outlying areas, how there is a culture of cronyism, and that officials are in place to bolster or be part of the NEC. He asserts their only interest is in what the SAFA life offers, in the form of honorariums and fancy trips, living it up. Most of the money used in the Regions is for administrative purposes and not for on the ground training.

The collateral damage, the young players who dream of a football career. Every other day, one of his players will call and ask when they will be playing in the league again, and he can’t give them an answer, because no one is responding to him, not at regional level or at National level. We speak to one of the players, whose dreams are frustrated. He talks about the challenges that he and his family face just to enable him to play, and now he can’t. Thabo takes us around the run down pitches and the villages where there is no football.

Thabo echoes the sentiments of many people we have spoken to from regional level to LFA’s, but fear to speak because of reprisal and victimisation from SAFA’s regional executives and those who are affiliated with them. They fear they can end up like Thabo, that once they speak out they will be targeted and their teams will suffer.

We meet Coach Junior from Mafikeng North West Province, who corroborates Thabo’s story and laments at the lack of support from the mother body SAFA. He describes how things have deteriorated over the years and that SAFA’s support has dwindled. That now the under 15’s and 17’s are chosen from the PSL only, so the talent scouts no longer find the future stars from ground up.

One of the main problems in developing football from the ground up is a lack of sponsorship, for prizes, kit and transport, medals etc. There was a time when the sponsors were there, Coca Cola, Sasol etc, all that’s left now is the ABC Motsepe League. This is not a local football problem, it goes all the way to the top.

SAFA found itself losing sponsors after the rape charges against Danny Jordaan in 2017. Dennis Mumble describes how major sponsors would only stay on if Danny Jordaan stepped down. After agreeing to do so, for the sake of football, a week before the SAFA elections in 2018, he retracted and decided to stand. This move is reflected in SAFA’s balance sheet, which dwindles from around 390 million rand per annum in revenue to it’s current 190 million per annum. Another example of how Jordaan has crafted the SAFA machine to suit his own needs and goals and not those for the support and development of the beautiful game.

Enter Bart Henderson – Forensic Auditor, whose High Level Risk Report on SAFA mismanagement and lack of governance, pointing to possible corruption and fraud by Danny Jordaan, has been met by SAFA laying charges of defamation and criminal charges, they say for transgressing the POPI Act.

Henderson points out the key issues for concern and what SAFA’s annual financials show in terms of their liquidity. This SAFA denies…


ACT 3

Meanwhile back at the Ranch – or should I rather say the White Elephant, the 67 million rand dud purchase..

Where did the Money go?

Presenter link – draw – Mooka vs Jordaan

Willie Mooka, former VP and Dennis Mumble opened a case against Danny Jordaan in 2021 – this included charges, one, of hiring a security and PR company solely for the purpose of managing allegations around rape charges by Jennifer Ferguson in 2018. Dennis Mumble opposed this and Danny Jordaan went over his head and authorised the money anyway. This is tantamount to fraud.

Bart explains why..

The other charge – the irregular way the FUN VALLEY property was purchased and where did the money go to once it had entered ENS Attorney’s account? The Hawks announced three years ago that arrests were imminent, yet to date no one has been arrested. Central figures were Gronie Hluyo CFO, and Danny Jordaan. Bizarrely the Hawks are supposedly interviewing people like Ivan Khoza who had nothing to do with the deal. It is unclear where the money went to after entering the ENS account. We will pose those questions directly to the Hawks.

Under a veil of secrecy and corporate mismanagement the Jordaan Fiefdom lives on. Changing rules before elections.. promising to stand down after the rape charges because sponsors were jittery, then going back on his word a week before elections – a seemingly unending thirst for control of the SAFA chairmanship – SA’s own Sep Blatter.

Why purchase a property that still needs so much work at a bloated price, in a location that is less than convenient for the National Players.. at this rate will they ever stay there?

SAFA recently announced that it needs a further 600 million to turn the facility into a World Class Centre. This vision they say, has been in the pipeline since 2015, but now SAFA will somehow raise the money this year, when their financials look dismal. Sponsorship has dwindled but they are counting now on FIFA grants – or loans...

The nay sayers believe this is not a reality based on past performance and SAFA’s current financial state.

We ask for SAFAs and Danny Jordaan’s ROR – with a request for a one on one interview with him based on the many allegations against him. An interview is not likely based on his previous responses. But I will try my hardest.

FINAL SCENE: We’re back on the ground with our budding football star and his final hopes for the future. The LFA Coach by his side.

Our young man indicates how his dream has been dashed – lack of funding – lack of support - The living Legacy that is no longer there for those who needed it.

We reflect on the lost legacy of the Legacy Trust that is no longer, and that for the last 13 years it was a cash cow for SAFA – bolstering it’s books as grants reflected as income and keeping afloat an organisation that has fared poorly in giving the 2010 World Cup a legacy that can live on.

The whistle-blowers which involve previous SAFA CEOs, Legacy Trust trustees and members of the NEC, allege they have been ignored or shut down by President of SAFA Danny Jordaan, and the CFO Gronie Hluyo over the years.

We ask the question – is it time for SAFA’s longest standing President to go?

Press Release:


In a village in Zeerust in the North West, 16-year-old Kutlwano Motswenyane plays soccer with his friends on a dusty field. He dreams of becoming an international football star. But with scarce resources in this community, his future is bleak. This shouldn’t be the case. In 2010, South Africa hosted the FIFA Soccer World Cup. One outcome of its success was a R450-million cash injection to form a Legacy Trust Fund to support and develop the game. The Legacy Trust should’ve become South Africa’s soccer heritage but, more than a decade later, it’s been milked dry, providing no benefit to players like Kutlwano.

Summary: 2010 was the year South Africa hosted the first FIFA World Cup held in Africa. A year of hope and optimism for a nation of soccer lovers. The reward from FIFA was 450 million rand in the form of a Legacy Trust Fund. Money that was meant to develop and support the game. Treasurer of the World Cup Committee at the time, Mohammed Mubarak, says it was a living annuity that should have earned interest in perpetuity. The interest generated year on year would have been enough to keep the development going, without touching the capital. In October 2021, the Legacy Trust Fund ran dry, closing its books with Five Million rand in the bank. SAFA sent its trustees packing without even a look-see at the final balance sheet. This was similar to the closure of the World Cup Committee in 2010, who never got to see the final balance sheets after the games ended. Carte Blanche exposes how a self-interested president, Danny Jordaan, has abused his authority and manipulated his stay in power at the expense of SAFA, putting at risk its ultimate goal - to support, uplift and develop the game of football in South Africa. How the Legacy Trust Fund was plundered and used as a cash cow for SAFA’s deteriorating balance sheet: As sponsors pulled out, after alleged rape charges against Danny Jordaan, so the Legacy Trust was dipped into more and more. And what was meant to be the jewel in the crown, the development of a world class training centre at Fun Valley Resort, South of Johannesburg, unearthed the rot. A controversial 67 million rand purchase that’s not fit for purpose and may never be. Again the Legacy Trust was used to fund this venture. But down the line the fallout reaches across the country, as aspirant young players are left to play on dusty pitches, with no kits or prizes, no transport to get to games - caught in a system that is crushing their football dreams. A system that mirrors the mother body in every way, where administrators hold on to power for perks and holidays, silencing detractors along the way. An old adage says: “The fish smells from the head”. Further information: Bart Henderson has been a forensic auditor for over 30 years. He lectures at the University of Pretoria and has worked on many prominent fraud and government corruption cases over the years. He uses data analysis to create a profile of the person(s) he is investigating. His mantra is – “I treat every sentence as a crime scene”. Bart has been involved in investigating the SAFA Legacy Trust Fund that was handed to SAFA after the 2010 World Cup - around R450 million Rand. He is baying for justice for the young up-and-coming sports stars that should have benefited from this legacy fund. The whistle-blowers which involve previous SAFA CEOs, Legacy Trust trustees and members of the NEC, allege they have been ignored or shut down by President of SAFA Danny Jordaan, and the CFO Gronie Hluyo over the years. The Legacy Trust was wound up in October 2021 without giving a final account of the remaining funds of 40 million Rands to the trustees, as they were relieved of their duties before it was wound up. Former SAFA Vice President and Legacy Trust trustee Ria Ledwaba says she has never seen the paperwork and when she requested it, she was told that she was no longer a trustee. According to her she never signed off the trust and if you look at the Master’s papers she is still listed as a trustee. According to Henderson, SAFA will not disclose a paper trail of how the funds were used for the Legacy Trust. The purchase of the Fun Valley Resort as a Training facility has been steeped in controversy. It was bought for a reported 67 million rand, but valued at 30 to 40. The deal was done through Ernst and Young and Cohen who was the seller – they, to this day, have not been able to produce evidence of where the money was deposited. There is a Hawks investigation that is ongoing and arrests were expected to be made a few years back, but nothing has happened. Former CEO Dennis Mumble gives a first hand account on how this property was purchased and how, after warning Danny Jordaan that it was a dud deal, he was shut out and the deal was put through. The Training Centre is not fit for purpose, and the South African official teams refuse to stay there. It apparently is only used occasionally for youth training programmes. It was supposed to be a world class training facility. Former Treasurer of the World Cup Committee, Mohammed Mubarak, attests to the purpose of the Legacy Trust and how it could have been the real saviour of football in South Africa, instead it was milked dry. He reflects on his brushings with Jordaan at the time and how when he was the treasurer of the World Cup Committee, he too was shut out when it came time to see the final balance sheets and bank statements. Even though he had resigned he remained treasurer to the end. SAFA has posted on their website, discrediting or trying to discredit Henderson. It is alleging that “former disgruntled officials of SAFA”, Henderson and a former trustee are trying to scupper the bid for the Women’s World Cup in 2027. It appears that this is the way that SAFA deals with detractors, they don’t answer questions from the media, even going as far as banning Daily Maverick and by attacking anyone who is exposing malfeasance. Henderson is not alone, there are many members who have served at SAFA willing to speak of the governance and alleged fraudulent activities conducted by SAFA under Danny Jordaan. For example according to Henderson, the current NEC has 47 members all of whom get paid a hundred thousand rand a year. They are merely there to be able to vote in SAFAs elections. In no other country are there so many NEC members, there are normally around 15, and FIFA recommended a reduction to 18, but that has never occurred. SAFA says they are cash strapped yet are not willing to make that kind of reduction, why? There has been an irregular turnover of CEOs, acting CEOs and Vice Presidents over the last few years, the question is why? The answer lies hidden in the loss of institutional memory. It’s harder for the naysayers to fight back. Money that is supposed to have been distributed to the regions for development purposes through the trust appears to still be outstanding, and the way the figures are put out fudge what is from the Legacy Trust and what is coming from SAFA’s obligatory contributions, according to Ria Ledwaba, a former SAFA Vice President and trustee of the Legacy Trust Fund. According to Mubarak and Henderson the Legacy Trust should have been a living trust where the original amount should not have been touched. If it had been put in a fixed deposit at 10% it would have earned 47 million a year that could go into development without touching the original funds. Yet now the Legacy Trust was depleted and closed with no public money trail. On the ground, virtually every region we spoke to at grass roots level is crying for support and grants from SAFA. In most cases they are afraid to speak out for fear of retribution, but one passionate excommunicated coach, Thabo Rabalao, is not afraid. He’s willing to put himself on the line for his teams and his players. Situated in the North West, in Zeerust, he gives us an inside view of the challenges he and his players face. The lack of facilities, sponsorship, kits and prizes, something that there used to be before. That after an illegal suspension, his young players are left with no leagues to play in. And that no one from the region right through to National even cares to respond to him after multiple appeals. We speak to one of his talented young players who feels that all his dreams are dashed. They even missed a selection a few weeks back because they are suspended and don’t have valid SAFA cards. We ask the question, why is there no legacy and no support for the footballers of the future? What role should SAFA be playing? SAFA is steeped in controversy and alleged misgovernance, with alleged fraudulent activity around Fun Valley and allegations by its former members. In 2010, South Africa hosted the FIFA Soccer World Cup. One outcome of its success was a R450-million cash injection to form a Legacy Trust Fund to support and develop the game. The Legacy Trust should’ve become South Africa’s soccer heritage but, more than a decade later, it’s been milked dry, providing no benefit to players like Kutlwano. Bart: I was originally approached by one of the trustees of the Legacy Trust, who had concerns in terms of the way the Legacy Trust was wound down whether there was any risk exposure to them VO: Bart Henderson is a forensic investigator targeting government and private corruption. Govan: What does that say to you? Bart: The revenue that has moved from the Legacy Trust to Safa has had a material impact on its bottom line. VO: Without that R65 million asset, SAFA's viability was at risk. Junior: Just look at our pitch, it tells you the story that you don't have nothing. Just look around, check our field you can see. This is a struggle brother, it’s a struggle. VO: In Mahikeng, Northwest, Coach Junior Morake leads a promising local female team, yet every day he feels he's on the losing side. Govan: Have you asked the region why they're not sending any money through or helping with any kit or transport? Junior: I’ve never asked them. Govan: Why not? Junior: Let me tell you something bra. You know football. Football is cruel. You ask something, it's like we are fighting. Govan: Fighting with who? Junior: with the leaders Govan: of the region? Junior: Yes. Govan: Do you think the problem is at a regional level? Junior: I think everybody in South Africa, they know the route, where it started. How can we at grassroot be okay, when the head is not functioning well? That's my question. Govan: You’re talking about the President Danny Jordaan? Junior: I talk about whoever's in charge of SAFA,, they might just look back and check where they come from. Have they done something for their community? Are they developing the young ones? BEAT// VO: So Is the World Cup’s only legacy - a trail of mistrust? //BEAT// Transition Ria: Until Danny Jordaan is out of SAFA and that organization is restructured properly, SAFA will still be where we are today. 10 years to come. VO: Whistleblowers are determined to challenge Jordaan's control. Ex-SAFA NEC member, MaleselaMooka, has lodged a criminal complaint against him for theft, fraud, and wasteful expenditure… Including issues around the Fun Valley purchase. Bart: All the projects that were funded with that 600 million must be audited, from cradle to grave// By the same token, the trustees of the Legacy Trust also had their own fiduciary duties. Your duty as a trustee is to protect the integrity of the trust. //BEAT// TRANSITION SAFA HOUSE Links Govan: Well, SAFA is refusing to respond to these damning allegations. And they say that's because some of these claims are subject to litigation. His lawyer confirmed with our producer minutes later. Lesedi: They forwarded me the list of questions which you sent a few days ago. And the position is that we would like to offer you an opportunity to meet with us during the course of next week. VO: But then they changed their mind. FRIDAY Lesedi: I’ve gotten proper instructions from client now after having looked at your questions, and the questions are all surrounding the FIFA Legacy Trust. Sophia: Correct. Lesedi: What you must remember is that the trust was a FIFA trust, it’s not a SAFA trust. Sophia: It's a SAFA-FIFA trust, that's what Mr. Jordaan texted… Lesedi: No, it’s a FIFA trust. Sophia: I'll give you Mr. Jordaan's exact words. Lesedi: When did Jordaan give you words? Sophia: He gave words to Govan. He said the Legacy Trust was a joint FIFA-SAFA trust. Lesedi: Let’s agree to disagree. VO: Citing legal action against Bart Henderson, they turned down our interview, directing us to FIFA. Sophia: Hold on. FIFA would would be able to answer the question as to when the last 40 million was wound down and those. Lesedi: FIFA ran the trust. So they are the perfect people to go to. VO: We wrote to FIFA. They said that "activities and projects funded by the Trust were submitted and reviewed by the Board of Trustees" and "compliance and auditing measures were in place". The Trust met its objectives and was closed down in compliance with South African Law. - and that was that! FIFA response (part) Activities and projects funded by the 2010 FIFA World Cup Legacy Trust were submitted and reviewed by the Board of Trustees, in accordance with South African law as well as the Trust’s overall objectives and compliance and auditing measures that were in place. After a successful delivery of these objectives over a number of years, the Trust was finally closed down in accordance with the relevant legislation. //BEAT// VO: But then another twist - // beat// We obtained a confidential document put out to the Regions,- the 2010 FIFA World Cup Legacy Trust Close Out Report, dated 2022 - sent out on the eve of our programme. // It showcases the Trust's achievements // but fudges on the detail. A glowing report, but not a full account… // and no apology for closing its doors, // BEAT// especially to grassroots footballers. Thabo: It's really frustrating, we are sometimes wondering what is it that we need to do? Or why is SAFA not investing a lot on grass roots, because that's where we unearth this talent. Kutlwano: I want to play overseas just like any other player out there. But currently from the area we are from it's hard for a player to finally reach professional. VO: As the final whistle blows, the only legacy that remains is loss. A loss for football - at its very heart.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In 2010, SA’s football loving nation was given the gift of hope – A Legacy Trust Fund– meant to develop the beautiful game. How did that 450 million rand become SAFA’s cash cow, milked dry?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The beans on SAFA’s mismanagement and bad governance have been spilled. With a virtually bankrupt balance sheet and a failure to develop football from ground up to National level, its President and chief for over a decade, Danny Jordaan, remains untouchable, winning election after election. How does he stay in control? Whistleblowers that have been victim to his manipulation speak out on camera. We don’t stop there, we expose how the rot has permeated the development of football at grass root level. Young football stars and wannabes who have been failed by the very body that is supposed to uplift them and the game.
metadata.Summary: 2010 was the year South Africa hosted the first FIFA World Cup held in Africa. A year of hope and optimism for a nation of soccer lovers. The reward from FIFA was 450 million rand in the form of a Legacy Trust Fund. Money that was meant to develop and support the game. Treasurer of the World Cup Committee at the time, Mohammed Mubarak, says it was a living annuity that should have earned interest in perpetuity. The interest generated year on year would have been enough to keep the development going, without touching the capital. In October 2021, the Legacy Trust Fund ran dry, closing its books with Five Million rand in the bank. SAFA sent its trustees packing without even a look-see at the final balance sheet. This was similar to the closure of the World Cup Committee in 2010, who never got to see the final balance sheets after the games ended. Carte Blanche exposes how a self-interested president, Danny Jordaan, has abused his authority and manipulated his stay in power at the expense of SAFA, putting at risk its ultimate goal - to support, uplift and develop the game of football in South Africa. How the Legacy Trust Fund was plundered and used as a cash cow for SAFA’s deteriorating balance sheet: As sponsors pulled out, after alleged rape charges against Danny Jordaan, so the Legacy Trust was dipped into more and more. And what was meant to be the jewel in the crown, the development of a world class training centre at Fun Valley Resort, South of Johannesburg, unearthed the rot. A controversial 67 million rand purchase that’s not fit for purpose and may never be. Again the Legacy Trust was used to fund this venture. But down the line the fallout reaches across the country, as aspirant young players are left to play on dusty pitches, with no kits or prizes, no transport to get to games - caught in a system that is crushing their football dreams. A system that mirrors the mother body in every way, where administrators hold on to power for perks and holidays, silencing detractors along the way. An old adage says: “The fish smells from the head”.
metadata.Further information: Bart Henderson has been a forensic auditor for over 30 years. He lectures at the University of Pretoria and has worked on many prominent fraud and government corruption cases over the years. He uses data analysis to create a profile of the person(s) he is investigating. His mantra is – “I treat every sentence as a crime scene”. Bart has been involved in investigating the SAFA Legacy Trust Fund that was handed to SAFA after the 2010 World Cup - around R450 million Rand. He is baying for justice for the young up-and-coming sports stars that should have benefited from this legacy fund. The whistle-blowers which involve previous SAFA CEOs, Legacy Trust trustees and members of the NEC, allege they have been ignored or shut down by President of SAFA Danny Jordaan, and the CFO Gronie Hluyo over the years. The Legacy Trust was wound up in October 2021 without giving a final account of the remaining funds of 40 million Rands to the trustees, as they were relieved of their duties before it was wound up. Former SAFA Vice President and Legacy Trust trustee Ria Ledwaba says she has never seen the paperwork and when she requested it, she was told that she was no longer a trustee. According to her she never signed off the trust and if you look at the Master’s papers she is still listed as a trustee. According to Henderson, SAFA will not disclose a paper trail of how the funds were used for the Legacy Trust. The purchase of the Fun Valley Resort as a Training facility has been steeped in controversy. It was bought for a reported 67 million rand, but valued at 30 to 40. The deal was done through Ernst and Young and Cohen who was the seller – they, to this day, have not been able to produce evidence of where the money was deposited. There is a Hawks investigation that is ongoing and arrests were expected to be made a few years back, but nothing has happened. Former CEO Dennis Mumble gives a first hand account on how this property was purchased and how, after warning Danny Jordaan that it was a dud deal, he was shut out and the deal was put through. The Training Centre is not fit for purpose, and the South African official teams refuse to stay there. It apparently is only used occasionally for youth training programmes. It was supposed to be a world class training facility. Former Treasurer of the World Cup Committee, Mohammed Mubarak, attests to the purpose of the Legacy Trust and how it could have been the real saviour of football in South Africa, instead it was milked dry. He reflects on his brushings with Jordaan at the time and how when he was the treasurer of the World Cup Committee, he too was shut out when it came time to see the final balance sheets and bank statements. Even though he had resigned he remained treasurer to the end. SAFA has posted on their website, discrediting or trying to discredit Henderson. It is alleging that “former disgruntled officials of SAFA”, Henderson and a former trustee are trying to scupper the bid for the Women’s World Cup in 2027. It appears that this is the way that SAFA deals with detractors, they don’t answer questions from the media, even going as far as banning Daily Maverick and by attacking anyone who is exposing malfeasance. Henderson is not alone, there are many members who have served at SAFA willing to speak of the governance and alleged fraudulent activities conducted by SAFA under Danny Jordaan. For example according to Henderson, the current NEC has 47 members all of whom get paid a hundred thousand rand a year. They are merely there to be able to vote in SAFAs elections. In no other country are there so many NEC members, there are normally around 15, and FIFA recommended a reduction to 18, but that has never occurred. SAFA says they are cash strapped yet are not willing to make that kind of reduction, why? There has been an irregular turnover of CEOs, acting CEOs and Vice Presidents over the last few years, the question is why? The answer lies hidden in the loss of institutional memory. It’s harder for the naysayers to fight back. Money that is supposed to have been distributed to the regions for development purposes through the trust appears to still be outstanding, and the way the figures are put out fudge what is from the Legacy Trust and what is coming from SAFA’s obligatory contributions, according to Ria Ledwaba, a former SAFA Vice President and trustee of the Legacy Trust Fund. According to Mubarak and Henderson the Legacy Trust should have been a living trust where the original amount should not have been touched. If it had been put in a fixed deposit at 10% it would have earned 47 million a year that could go into development without touching the original funds. Yet now the Legacy Trust was depleted and closed with no public money trail. On the ground, virtually every region we spoke to at grass roots level is crying for support and grants from SAFA. In most cases they are afraid to speak out for fear of retribution, but one passionate excommunicated coach, Thabo Rabalao, is not afraid. He’s willing to put himself on the line for his teams and his players. Situated in the North West, in Zeerust, he gives us an inside view of the challenges he and his players face. The lack of facilities, sponsorship, kits and prizes, something that there used to be before. That after an illegal suspension, his young players are left with no leagues to play in. And that no one from the region right through to National even cares to respond to him after multiple appeals. We speak to one of his talented young players who feels that all his dreams are dashed. They even missed a selection a few weeks back because they are suspended and don’t have valid SAFA cards. We ask the question, why is there no legacy and no support for the footballers of the future? What role should SAFA be playing? SAFA is steeped in controversy and alleged misgovernance, with alleged fraudulent activity around Fun Valley and allegations by its former members. The collateral damage is to “football”. We put these serious questions to the man at the helm, its President, Danny Jordaan. INTERVIEWS: EXPERTS: 1. BART HENDERSON – FORENSIC AUDITOR 2. MOHAMMED MUBARAK – FORMER 2010 WORLD CUP COMMITTEE, TREASURER CASE STUDIES: 3. DENNIS MUMBLE- SAFA FORMER CEO 4. GAY MOKOENA – SAFA FORMER VP/CEO 5. RIA LEDWABA – SAFA FORMER VP, LEGACY TRUST TRUSTEE 6. COACH THABO RABALAO – RAMOLFA CLUBS, ZEERUST, NORTH WEST PROVINCE 7. COACH JUNIOR – MAFIKENG 8. PLAYER- COACH THABO 9. DANNY JORDAAN – PRESIDENT SAFA - SAFA SPOKESPERSON MINA NHLOKWE TREATMENT Treatment Summary: The story will be told through the central character – SAFA’s white elephant - Fun Valley. 38 Hectares of land, nestled between Lenasia and Soweto, a dream in the making, a hotel, refurbished rooms, a football pitch or two, this is the 87 million rand or so home - for the South African Football Association’s Technical Centre purchased in 2015. The vision – A world class Technical Training Facility able to host National and international teams. As in knockout football tournaments, the visual device I want to use is the presenter putting their hand in a bag.. as in picking a draw.. and pulling out a ball. Each ball has a name on it – and each ‘fixture’ will highlight key issues – eg ‘Danny Jordaan vs the Legacy Trust’. ‘Mumble vs Jordaan’, etc.. The presenter calls the draw, and each ‘match’ is an element of the story we are highlighting - turns to another camera to take us back into the narrative.. audio with audio transitions of football crowds cheering .. singing or jeering in disappointment.. The links will be done in a studio-like setting… as one would a draw.. Visual narrative will be built through three teenagers kicking a soccer ball down a dusty road – two boys and a girl – the scenes will be moody and dark.. often just focusing on their faces .. when we talk about legacy or development.. a slow-mo shot of a football tumbling through the air.. etc.. With some possible archive of football matches from SuperSport as well? We also have paper trail evidence – minutes of meetings etc.. emails to back what the whistle-blowers are saying. Some recreations/ dramatisations – nuanced and not overt – that reflect some of the dealings behind closed doors etc... ACT 1 We take a stay for a night at Fun Valley, although it may be fit for a tourist for a night or two, it currently does not have nearly the facilities and amenities to make it world class. But is it and when will it ever be fit for purpose? Dennis Mumble VP under Danny Jordaan was the man instructed to conclude the deal. Dennis describes the circumstances that led to a purchase of a property that cost double the evaluation price. He takes a journey with us to Fun Valley, here he describes how Cohen the seller, after the poor valuation told him to take the deal or leave it. Presenter Link – Draw – Mumble vs Jordaan Mumble highlights to Jordaan why this is a bad deal and it is overpriced. How Jordaan bull-dosed the deal through the NEC and the Trust without due diligence or adhering to proper corporate governance. ( First hand account) This story is backed by Shuping Seboko who served as a member of the NEC at the time. Ria Ledwaba – Trustee and Former VP of SAFA – backs this up on how it was announced at a Trustee meeting that the NEC had approved the purchase of the property and that the trust was to make the money available – the normal practice is for SAFA to apply to the Trust for funding. This did not occur – nor was there a discussion with the NEC about the purchase – it was announced at the NEC that the funds had been made available by the Trust for this purpose – to buy Fun Valley. ACT 2 Our story will take us back to 2010 where the Legacy Trust was formed and its intended purpose. Here Mohammed Mubarak the treasurer of the SAFA 2010 Committee – gives us the inside track and we see how history repeats itself – VO: Since the 2010 World Cup that put South Africa centre stage – SAFA has been mired in controversy – at its helm Chairman Danny Jordaan. Presenter Link: putting his hand in a black bag and mixing the balls – presenter makes the draw and reads: “[Mokoena?/] Mubarak” .. “vesus” .. “Jordaan” [Mokoena?/] Mubarak - treasurer of the 2010 World Cup Committee, talks about how devastating the bribery allegations have been to SAFA and how he was shut out before the final financial tally after the World Cup ended, even though he had been the treasurer throughout. He talks about how, then, Danny Jordaan started shaping his fiefdom, removing all detractors and scrutinisors. He throws forward to the Legacy Trust that should have kept football alive if only they had just used the 10% interest generated annually from the 450 million – it could still be in existence. He was relieved of his duties as treasurer of the 2010 World Cup Committee before the final financial tallies were made.. even though he had resigned, Mubarak remained treasurer until the end, but was never allowed to see the books he had administered. Here Mubarak talks passionately about the development of football in South Africa, and how SAFA has misused the Legacy Trust.. MOKOENA: Former VP and acting CEO: SAFA RIA: talks about the irregular way the trust was closed and how she never got to see the final financials, as the trustees were relieved of their positions before that was done. The only Trustee left to wind things up was not even someone with a financial background. FIFA was unhappy with how it was done and there are emails to prove this. The trust was dissolved in 2021 with only five million Rand in the kitty – Presenter link – the draw: SAFA vs Development Thabo Rabalao is a club owner of an LFA in Zeerust, North West Province. He is passionate about the development of youth football. Due to a disagreement with the Region, he and his teams have been suspended from the SAFA leagues for over 7 months. This is unconstitutional according to the LFA and regional constitution which states that a team or person cannot be suspended for longer than 3 months if a matter has not been resolved. Thabo describes how the regional SAFA officials are not interested in developing the game, especially in outlying areas, how there is a culture of cronyism, and that officials are in place to bolster or be part of the NEC. He asserts their only interest is in what the SAFA life offers, in the form of honorariums and fancy trips, living it up. Most of the money used in the Regions is for administrative purposes and not for on the ground training. The collateral damage, the young players who dream of a football career. Every other day, one of his players will call and ask when they will be playing in the league again, and he can’t give them an answer, because no one is responding to him, not at regional level or at National level. We speak to one of the players, whose dreams are frustrated. He talks about the challenges that he and his family face just to enable him to play, and now he can’t. Thabo takes us around the run down pitches and the villages where there is no football. Thabo echoes the sentiments of many people we have spoken to from regional level to LFA’s, but fear to speak because of reprisal and victimisation from SAFA’s regional executives and those who are affiliated with them. They fear they can end up like Thabo, that once they speak out they will be targeted and their teams will suffer. We meet Coach Junior from Mafikeng North West Province, who corroborates Thabo’s story and laments at the lack of support from the mother body SAFA. He describes how things have deteriorated over the years and that SAFA’s support has dwindled. That now the under 15’s and 17’s are chosen from the PSL only, so the talent scouts no longer find the future stars from ground up. One of the main problems in developing football from the ground up is a lack of sponsorship, for prizes, kit and transport, medals etc. There was a time when the sponsors were there, Coca Cola, Sasol etc, all that’s left now is the ABC Motsepe League. This is not a local football problem, it goes all the way to the top. SAFA found itself losing sponsors after the rape charges against Danny Jordaan in 2017. Dennis Mumble describes how major sponsors would only stay on if Danny Jordaan stepped down. After agreeing to do so, for the sake of football, a week before the SAFA elections in 2018, he retracted and decided to stand. This move is reflected in SAFA’s balance sheet, which dwindles from around 390 million rand per annum in revenue to it’s current 190 million per annum. Another example of how Jordaan has crafted the SAFA machine to suit his own needs and goals and not those for the support and development of the beautiful game. Enter Bart Henderson – Forensic Auditor, whose High Level Risk Report on SAFA mismanagement and lack of governance, pointing to possible corruption and fraud by Danny Jordaan, has been met by SAFA laying charges of defamation and criminal charges, they say for transgressing the POPI Act. Henderson points out the key issues for concern and what SAFA’s annual financials show in terms of their liquidity. This SAFA denies… ACT 3 Meanwhile back at the Ranch – or should I rather say the White Elephant, the 67 million rand dud purchase.. Where did the Money go? Presenter link – draw – Mooka vs Jordaan Willie Mooka, former VP and Dennis Mumble opened a case against Danny Jordaan in 2021 – this included charges, one, of hiring a security and PR company solely for the purpose of managing allegations around rape charges by Jennifer Ferguson in 2018. Dennis Mumble opposed this and Danny Jordaan went over his head and authorised the money anyway. This is tantamount to fraud. Bart explains why.. The other charge – the irregular way the FUN VALLEY property was purchased and where did the money go to once it had entered ENS Attorney’s account? The Hawks announced three years ago that arrests were imminent, yet to date no one has been arrested. Central figures were Gronie Hluyo CFO, and Danny Jordaan. Bizarrely the Hawks are supposedly interviewing people like Ivan Khoza who had nothing to do with the deal. It is unclear where the money went to after entering the ENS account. We will pose those questions directly to the Hawks. Under a veil of secrecy and corporate mismanagement the Jordaan Fiefdom lives on. Changing rules before elections.. promising to stand down after the rape charges because sponsors were jittery, then going back on his word a week before elections – a seemingly unending thirst for control of the SAFA chairmanship – SA’s own Sep Blatter. Why purchase a property that still needs so much work at a bloated price, in a location that is less than convenient for the National Players.. at this rate will they ever stay there? SAFA recently announced that it needs a further 600 million to turn the facility into a World Class Centre. This vision they say, has been in the pipeline since 2015, but now SAFA will somehow raise the money this year, when their financials look dismal. Sponsorship has dwindled but they are counting now on FIFA grants – or loans... The nay sayers believe this is not a reality based on past performance and SAFA’s current financial state. We ask for SAFAs and Danny Jordaan’s ROR – with a request for a one on one interview with him based on the many allegations against him. An interview is not likely based on his previous responses. But I will try my hardest. FINAL SCENE: We’re back on the ground with our budding football star and his final hopes for the future. The LFA Coach by his side. Our young man indicates how his dream has been dashed – lack of funding – lack of support - The living Legacy that is no longer there for those who needed it. We reflect on the lost legacy of the Legacy Trust that is no longer, and that for the last 13 years it was a cash cow for SAFA – bolstering it’s books as grants reflected as income and keeping afloat an organisation that has fared poorly in giving the 2010 World Cup a legacy that can live on. The whistle-blowers which involve previous SAFA CEOs, Legacy Trust trustees and members of the NEC, allege they have been ignored or shut down by President of SAFA Danny Jordaan, and the CFO Gronie Hluyo over the years. We ask the question – is it time for SAFA’s longest standing President to go?
